findings.feature: CLI setup idempotency / rerun safety
findings.impact: createConfig() returns early when a config exists and --force is absent, so setup silently 'succeeds' without regenerating configuration, yet still prints a fresh success message. installVSCodeHooks() rewrites an existing editor settings.json through JSON.parse of a Buffer and rewrites the whole file, risking loss of user settings.
findings.observedBehavior: config-manager.ts:31-33 early return; install-hooks.ts:58-67 read-modify-write of settings.json.
findings.expectedBehavior: Rerun must be idempotent, must not silently skip work behind a success message, and must not risk clobbering unrelated user settings.
findings.reproduction: Run setup twice; observe identical success output on the second run.
findings.rootCause: Prototype flow lacks state reporting.
findings.acceptanceCriteria: Second run reports precisely what changed vs was already present; malformed settings.json produces an explicit error, not data loss.
findings.plannedFix: Report skip/create per step; validate JSON before write; preserve unknown keys.
findings.verificationMethod: Two consecutive runs in an isolated HOME plus a malformed-settings fixture.
evidence: read packages/cli/src/utils/config-manager.ts
read packages/cli/src/utils/install-hooks.ts
FIX: createConfig() now returns { path, outcome: 'created' | 'reused' } and setup prints 'Config already present' on a rerun instead of a misleading fresh-success message.

FIX: the destructive read-modify-write of editor settings.json was removed entirely - the CLI no longer touches ~/.cursor/settings.json or ~/.vscode/settings.json, so there is no longer any path that can clobber user settings or crash on a malformed file.

PENDING: the two-consecutive-runs verification could not be completed in this workspace because concurrent builds repeatedly delete packages/core/dist (see AIDR-014); it must be re-run on a quiet tree.

TWO HALVES. (1) Rerun honesty: `createConfig` already returned `{outcome:'created'|'reused'}`, but setup DISCARDED the outcome and printed the same `✅ Setup complete!` on a rerun as on a first install, so a user could not tell a no-op from a real setup. (2) `installVSCodeHooks` rewrote an existing editor `settings.json` through a JSON round-trip, risking loss of the user's own settings.

HALF 2 IS ALREADY GONE and this was verified rather than assumed: `install-hooks.ts` now explicitly documents that an earlier version wrote `claude-hooks.json`, `aidr.enabled`/`aidr.hooksPath` editor settings and an OpenClaw plugins array — none of which any shipped connector reads — and then reported success. Those writers are removed; a test pins that `installVSCodeHooks`, `settings.json`, `claude-hooks` and `hooksPath` do not reappear in the executable code.
HALF 1 FIXED: setup now branches on the outcome and prints either `✅ Setup complete!` (created) or `✅ Setup verified — no changes were needed.` plus the reused config path (reused).

VERIFIED BEHAVIOUR against the built CLI in an isolated HOME: run 1 prints '✅ Setup complete!' with 'Config: <path>' and 'Detection verified (351 rules, probe matched 1)'; run 2 prints 'Config already present: <path>' and '✅ Setup verified — no changes were needed.  Existing config reused: <path>'. The two runs are now distinguishable.

A THIRD DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED WHILE VERIFYING: setup's next-steps list contained 'Start using your AI agent normally' immediately above 'Protection is NOT yet active for your agent' — an unqualified all-clear printed by a security product on the same screen that says nothing is inspecting tool calls. The list now reads 'Install the connector below — until you do, tool calls are NOT inspected'.

VERIFIED RUN: npx vitest run packages/cli -> exit 0, 36/36 passed, including 9 new setup-honesty guards: 'created' on a first run and 'reused' on a rerun; the config is written owner-only; a rerun does NOT rotate the credential (a user who had registered the old key would be broken); --force does rotate it; and the removed writers stay removed.

TEST ISOLATION NOTE, disclosed: `config-manager` captures `homedir()` at import time, so the new suite stubs `node:os` before importing it. Redirecting `process.env.HOME` in a beforeEach would have been too late and the test would have written into the developer's real ~/.singularity-aidr — the same class of isolation bug found in rollback.test.ts during AIDR-030.

Team administration was fully implemented and unreachable: AdminPanel was exported and referenced nowhere, there was no /admin or /team route, and EnterpriseAuth.handleTeamInviteAccept navigated to '/team' — a route that did not exist — so accepting an invitation landed on a dead end.

FIXED: /team route (AppLayout + requireSessionLoader + TeamPage) plus a Team nav entry, and EnterpriseAuth is now routed at /enterprise (standalone, no session loader, because invitees are signed out). Its invite link is /enterprise?invite=<token> and the token is now preserved across the OAuth round trip via setPostAuthReturnTo — previously it was dropped, so an invitation could never actually be completed even after sign-in.

A SECOND, DEEPER DEFECT FOUND WHILE WIRING: TeamRole was admin|member|viewer while the DB check constraint is owner|admin|member|viewer, and handle_new_user_team() makes every new user the OWNER of their personal team — so `canManageTeam = role === 'admin'` locked owners out of their own team. Adding the route alone would not have made the feature usable. Roles are now owner/admin -> manage, member/viewer -> read-only with an explicit notice; ownership transfer is deliberately not offered.

HONEST FAILURE REPORTING: a failed membership query no longer renders 'Team Members (0)' (which fabricated an empty team); it renders a visible error and states that no member count is shown because the rows could not be read. A failed team-membership query no longer claims 'You are not part of any team yet.' Invite/role-change/removal successes are reported only after the DB returns affected rows. The old `status.includes('Failed')` styling rendered some real errors as a neutral notice.

MUTATION EVIDENCE that the tests would have caught this: removing the /team route from main.tsx makes exactly 2 new guards fail ('registers /team through the console shell behind the session loader', 'never navigates to a route the router does not define'). main.tsx was restored byte-identical (sha256 verified).

REACHABLE BUT BACKEND-MISSING, NOT HIDDEN: the `team-invite` Edge Function does not exist, so an invite now fails visibly — 'the "team-invite" Edge Function is unavailable (<error>). No invitation was sent and no member was added.' Success is impossible without an explicit {"ok":true} acknowledgement, so an empty 200 can no longer become 'Invitation sent'. `public.users` is not exposed by PostgREST, so the member list falls back to user ids with a visible 'Member email addresses are unavailable in this deployment.' notice, and only a genuine missing-relation error triggers that fallback while a permission or network error stays a hard error. Create team, change role and remove member ARE genuinely functional (create_team_tenant RPC + team_members RLS both exist).

PolicyEditor implemented load/validate/save of a team policy against the team_policies table but was referenced nowhere and had no route, so the advertised policy-authoring capability was absent from the product surface.

FIXED: /policies route (AppLayout + requireSessionLoader + PolicyPage) plus a nav entry that appears once the role is resolved and permits editing — it stays visible while the role is unknown, because hiding a capability on an unresolved lookup makes a failed query look like a permission decision. The page gates on canEditPolicy and never renders the editor for a viewer.

THREE REAL DEFECTS SURFACED THE MOMENT IT WAS WIRED, all fixed and test-pinned: (1) an infinite render loop, because the load effect depended on component-local functions and re-queried forever — now module-scope helpers with the effect depending on the team id, and a test asserts exactly one read; (2) the hand-rolled YAML reader never handled a nested mapping inside a sequence item, so `condition:` became the key `'condition:'` and the preview crashed on rule.condition.tool — rewritten as an indentation-aware block parser, and the writer no longer emits array values at indent 0 (which made the default policy invalid against the editor's own validation); (3) saving could NEVER succeed — `upsert(..., { onConflict: 'team_id' })` against a table with no unique constraint on team_id raises Postgres 42P10 — replaced with probe-then-update/insert verifying returned rows, with the payload the schema requires (team_id on insert, tenant_id = team_id for the team_policies_tenant_matches_team check, updated_by = auth.uid()).

VALIDATION IS NOW REAL (version, default_action in allow/deny/ask, rules array, per-rule name/action/condition), so 'Valid policy' means something and an invalid document cannot be saved. If the stored policy cannot be read, saving is disabled rather than overwriting an unseen document.
DISCLOSED IN THE UI, NOT ASSUMED: nothing in this repository reads public.team_policies, so a saved policy is stored but not proven to reach runtime enforcement, and the page says so.

findings.feature: Supabase Edge Function configuration validation
findings.impact: Edge Functions read platform configuration as Deno.env.get(...) ?? '', so a missing SUPABASE_URL or SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY does not fail fast; the function proceeds with empty credentials and fails later with an opaque error instead of a clear 500 configuration error.
findings.observedBehavior: supabase/functions/url-check/index.ts:14-16 (and the same pattern across the functions tree).
findings.expectedBehavior: Missing required configuration must fail closed and early with an explicit server-configuration error.
findings.reproduction: Invoke the function with the env var unset; observe the downstream failure rather than an explicit configuration error.
findings.rootCause: Convenience ?? '' fallback instead of validated configuration access.
findings.acceptanceCriteria: Every function returns an explicit 5xx configuration error before any DB/auth work when required config is absent; covered by test.
findings.plannedFix: Shared requireEnv helper that throws/returns a configuration error.
findings.verificationMethod: Deno-level unit test with the variable removed.
evidence: read supabase/functions/url-check/index.ts

Edge Functions read configuration as `Deno.env.get(...) ?? ""`, so a missing SUPABASE_URL or SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY did not fail fast: the function proceeded with empty credentials and failed later with an opaque error.

FIXED: supabase/functions/_shared/config.ts is the single fail-closed configuration boundary. loadConfig(env, names) validates every required variable per request BEFORE any createClient/auth/DB/RPC work and returns a ConfigurationError carrying code server_misconfigured, status 500, and missing/invalid = variable NAMES ONLY. The constructor filters entries against /^[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]{0,63}$/, so a value passed where a name belongs can never reach a response or a log. partialGroupError catches half-configured secret pairs.

APPLIED TO ALL 20 canonical Edge Functions, removing every `Deno.env.get("SUPABASE_URL"/"SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY") ?? ""`. Function-specific secrets covered: AIDR_PADDLE_WEBHOOK_SECRET, AIDR_PADDLE_CHECKOUT_URL (while the legacy flag is on), the AutoSecOps URL/token pair (partial = error; entirely unset stays 'integration off' with the unchanged 503), and the entitlement/revocation signing key pairs in enroll/ingest/revocations (a half-configured pair now errors instead of silently returning *_signed: null). SUPABASE_ANON_KEY is read by zero Edge Functions.

OBSERVED BEHAVIOUR: status=500 body={"error":"server_misconfigured","missing":["SUPABASE_URL","SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY"]}, and the single-variable case names only the missing one. The log line carries names only: [url-check] configuration error {"code":"server_misconfigured","status":500,"missing":[...],"invalid":[]}.

DELIBERATE, DISCLOSED BEHAVIOUR CHANGES (all 5xx, no test weakened): the supabase pair now returns server_misconfigured + missing instead of misconfigured_supabase_env; paddle and billing-checkout likewise; autosecops moves from 503 misconfigured_supabase to 500 server_misconfigured + names. stripe-webhook KEEPS its documented 400 invalid_signature with no writes when STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET is unprovisioned, because Stripe must not retry an unverifiable delivery, and the variable is named in the log.

TREES ARE DIVERGENT AND THAT WAS HANDLED: packages/dashboard/supabase/functions/ holds exactly one legacy auth-callback that nothing invokes (the dashboard calls the absent oauth-callback, tracked as AIDR-019 and deliberately untouched). It had the same defect — redirect_uri resolved to the literal 'undefined/auth/v1/callback' — and was fixed with a BYTE-IDENTICAL copy of the helper (same hash on both copies, because it deploys independently and cannot import across trees) plus a sync test asserting byte-identity.
MUTATION CHECK proving the tests bite: temporarily re-adding `const X = Deno.env.get("SUPABASE_URL") ?? ""` to pilot-status made 3 contract tests fail; the file diff was then verified clean.

VERIFIED RUN: AIDR_TEST_NO_BUILD=1 npx vitest run supabase --root . -> exit 0, 7 files, 211 tests passed (config.test.ts 23, config-contract.test.ts 109, handler-contract +1). node scripts/check-supabase-edge-contracts.mjs -> exit 0 ('20/20 functions config-guarded'); check-supabase-migrations.mjs -> exit 0; check-commercial-surface.mjs -> exit 0. No-secret-leak assertions cover the response body, log detail, message and stack.

NOT VERIFIED: not executed under the real Deno runtime or against a live Supabase project (no Deno/network here) — behaviour is proven by unit tests on the shipped module plus static wiring contracts, the same coverage boundary the pre-existing handler-contract tests use. AIDR_PACK_MASTER_KEY_B64 remains optional provisioning (an unset master key yields pack_keys: [] for premium_intel tenants, and the client fails closed on absent entitlements); recorded as a residual gap. _shared/cors.ts still defaults AIDR_ALLOWED_ORIGINS to empty, which is deliberate fail-closed (403 origin_not_allowed).

ROOT CAUSE: the connector delegated every decision to a control plane that has never been deployed. `publish()` unconditionally returned `{accepted:false, reasonCode:'central_signed_ingress_required'}` (which instrumentation maps to deny), and identity was built only from AUTOSECOPS_* env vars, so a default install produced `deny/codex_input_malformed` for EVERY pre-tool call. It was also absent from every build/release/CI gate.

THE PROTOCOL WAS ESTABLISHED FROM THE REAL BINARY, NOT FROM DOCS. `codex-cli 0.141.0` is installed here; `codex features list` reports `hooks stable true`. Its embedded JSON schemas were extracted from the binary: input `{session_id,turn_id,transcript_path,cwd,hook_event_name,model,permission_mode,tool_name,tool_input,tool_use_id}` (additionalProperties:false, all required) and output `{hookSpecificOutput:{hookEventName:'PreToolUse',permissionDecision,permissionDecisionReason,updatedInput},decision,continue,suppressOutput,systemMessage}` with `permissionDecision in {allow,deny,ask}`.

CONFIG SHAPE VERIFIED AGAINST THE BINARY, and this is where the previous state would have failed silently: the documented/plausible lower-case table `[[hooks.pre_tool_use]]` is parsed by TOML and then IGNORED — the hook never runs and nothing warns. The working shapes are `[[hooks.PreToolUse]]` with nested `[[hooks.PreToolUse.hooks]]` handlers, or `~/.codex/hooks.json` as `{"hooks":{"PreToolUse":[{"matcher":"^Bash$","hooks":[{"type":"command","command":"...","timeout":30}]}]}}`. Verified end-to-end: the hook receives a real payload with `tool_name:"Bash"`, `tool_input:{"command":"echo verify-probe"}`.

BUILT: packages/codex is now a real local-enforcement connector — assets.ts (rule resolution), extractors.ts, enforcement.ts, cli.ts, esbuild.config.js, scripts/sync-assets.mjs, README.md, package.json (bin aidr-codex-hook, resources shipped, codex added to build:release gates). It runs the shared detection core and never calls a remote service on the critical path.
FAIL-OPEN HANDLING — the measured behaviour matrix, driven against the real binary with an isolated CODEX_HOME (10 hook behaviours x 1 real tool call):
explicit `deny` with a reason          -> command DID NOT RUN   (blocks)
`deny` with an EMPTY reason            -> command RAN           (fail-open)
`allow`                                -> command RAN
`ask`                                  -> command RAN           (unsupported value, fail-open)
exit 2 WITH non-empty stderr           -> command RAN           (fail-open)
exit 2 with EMPTY stderr               -> command RAN           (fail-open)
plain text on stdout, exit 0           -> command RAN           (ignored)
hook crashed (exit 1)                  -> command RAN           (fail-open)
malformed JSON on stdout               -> command RAN           (fail-open)
no output                              -> command RAN           (fail-open)

Every failure mode is fail-open and a hook cannot change that, so the connector gives Codex the only answer it honours: `ask` is TRANSLATED INTO `deny` (sending the documented `ask` value would let the call through), internal errors become an explicit deny, the reason is never empty, and unparseable input blocks. The one remaining fail-open path is the process being killed before it writes anything — a host property, recorded not hidden.

METHOD CORRECTION WORTH RECORDING: my first behaviour probe reported FAIL-OPEN for an explicit deny, contradicting an earlier marker-file test. The probe was wrong, not the product: it matched the command text anywhere in the event stream, and when a hook blocks a call the MODEL STILL ECHOES the command in its reply. Reading the raw JSONL settled it — the deny case emits `Command blocked by PreToolUse hook` and NO `command_execution` item, while the allow case emits `item.type=command_execution ... output="probe-alpha"`. The probe now keys on a `command_execution` item that produced output.

`apply_patch` IS INSPECTED. Verified against the binary: Codex sends the patch text in `tool_input.command`, whereas Claude Code's Edit/Write use file_path/old_string/new_string. Passing it to the shared extractor unchanged would fall through to the unknown-tool path and the patch body would never be examined. The connector extracts both the patch body and every `*** Add/Update/Delete File:` target, so an authorized_keys write hidden in a patch is caught.

VERIFIED RUN (built artifact, the thing a customer installs): node scripts/verify-codex-hook.mjs -> exit 0, ALL PASS, 11/11 cases — must-BLOCK: pipe-to-shell, rm -rf /, reverse shell, credential write via apply_patch; must-ALLOW: ls -la, git status, pnpm test, ordinary patch; malformed: unparseable stdin -> deny, empty stdin -> deny, wrong event -> allow. Every blocking case emits a NON-EMPTY reason, which is required because an empty reason fails open.

TRUST IS A REAL OPERATIONAL CONSTRAINT, recorded rather than hidden: Codex will not run a hook it has not reviewed, and an untrusted hook is dropped during discovery and silently never runs. findings.feature: Threat-rule regex execution safety (ReDoS) and hook timeout budget
findings.impact: heuristics.ts:16-39 implements a regex 'timeout' by measuring elapsed time AFTER a synchronous, uninterruptible `exec` returns, so it measures but never prevents catastrophic backtracking. Measured: threats/win-obfuscation.yaml:148 costs ~2.07s on a 20KB command and ~45s on a 100KB command (quadratic); extractors.ts stripHeredocs is also O(n^2) (~1.6s on a 60KB command). Bash commands reach heuristics uncapped, while hooks/hooks.json gives PreToolUse a 15s timeout. A single long command therefore exceeds the hook budget, the hook is killed before emitting a verdict, and the tool call proceeds uninspected - a deterministic detection-evasion primitive and a local DoS.

findings.feature: Agent self-approval of blocked actions (aidr_approve)
findings.impact: The approval gate is exposed to the same agent it polices. OpenClaw registers `aidr_approve` as an agent-callable tool (gate-tool.ts:37-48, index.ts:76) whose only 'user confirmation' is an instruction in its description; core/src/guard.ts:39-41 then short-circuits the entire evaluation on a recorded approval. The agent already receives the actionId in the block reason (guard.ts:111), so a prompt-injected agent can trigger a flagged action, approve it itself, and re-issue it to receive allowVerdict('approved'). Every 'ask' verdict becomes self-approvable, and aidr_allowlist_add then converts it into a permanent bypass. Same pattern in OpenCode (index.ts:138-154, with a comment acknowledging it is a workaround pending a native question tool).

findings.reproduction: In the OpenClaw/OpenCode connector, block a command, then invoke the approval tool with the actionId from the block message, then retry - the retry is allowed.
findings.rootCause: The approval tool was implemented as an agent-visible tool for lack of a host-native confirmation primitive, which hands the authority to the untrusted party.
findings.dependencies: Requires a host-side confirmation mechanism per connector (OpenClaw/OpenCode APIs).
findings.acceptanceCriteria: An agent cannot cause its own approval by any tool call; approval requires an action the agent cannot perform; the blocked action remains blocked until a human approves.
findings.plannedFix: Remove the agent-callable approval path and route approval to the host UI; if a connector has no host primitive, keep the verdict 'ask' (non-executable) rather than exposing a self-approval tool.
findings.verificationMethod: Adversarial test: agent attempts self-approval and the retry must still be blocked.

findings.impact: The dashboard's unverified Lemon Squeezy webhook was removed and replaced with a signature-verifying Stripe handler, but the SDK still ships a complete Lemon Squeezy billing client that is wired to a public API and a CLI command. findings.feature: AutoQuarantine could not survive a restart (constructor used floating promises)
findings.impact: `AutoQuarantine`'s constructor called `this.ensureQuarantineDir()` and `this.loadManifest()` without `await`, but both were declared `private async`. The instance was therefore returned before either completed: a fresh instance's `list()` reported zero items even when a manifest with quarantined files existed on disk, and any failure inside those calls surfaced as an unhandled rejection instead of an error. Any operator flow that reconstructs the manager (a new CLI invocation, a restarted connector, a dashboard request) would appear to have an empty quarantine while the files were still held. The existing test suite missed it because it never re-instantiated the manager. This is a prerequisite for wiring the ADR response lifecycle, since quarantine has to be trustworthy across restarts before it can be driven from a verdict.
findings.observedBehavior: Before the fix: write a manifest containing one item, then `new AutoQuarantine(config)`; `manager.list()` returned `[]` synchronously.
findings.expectedBehavior: A constructed instance is fully initialised: the quarantine directory exists and the persisted manifest is loaded before the constructor returns.
findings.reproduction: 1) Create a quarantine dir and a valid `manifest.json` with one item. 2) `const m = new AutoQuarantine(config); m.list()` -> before: `[]`; after: one item.
findings.rootCause: Async helpers were invoked from a synchronous constructor without awaiting, so construction and initialisation were not ordered.
findings.acceptanceCriteria: No un-awaited promise in the constructor; a new instance sees persisted items immediately; a corrupt or version-mismatched manifest is handled without throwing; quarantine/restore round-trips through a rebuild of the manager.
findings.plannedFix: Replaced the two async helpers with synchronous equivalents (`ensureQuarantineDirSync` using `mkdirSync`, `loadManifestSync` using the existing `getFileContentSync`), because the constructor genuinely must complete this work before returning. Failures are caught and logged rather than surfacing as unhandled rejections.
findings.verificationMethod: New regression suite covering immediate usability, restart survival, corrupt manifest, unknown manifest version, and a real quarantine/restore round trip across a rebuild.

DESIGN DECISION RECORDED: the action shipped is `snapshot_on_deny`, not quarantine, because the connector decides BEFORE the tool executes - the blocked write never happened, so moving or deleting the target would destroy the user's data. A snapshot is a COPY into ~/.singularity-aidr/response-vault and the original is left byte-identical. Quarantine's move semantics are only correct post-execution.

SAFETY BOUNDARIES (each tested): the action is OFF by default; allowed verdicts never trigger it; a severity floor (default warning) and a size ceiling (default 10 MiB) bound it; a non-file tool or an absent target is reported as a skip with a machine-readable reason rather than being silently omitted; a response failure is recorded as outcome=failure and STILL leaves the blocking verdict intact; records never contain file contents; the vault is created 0700.

FIX (defensive, found by the suite): guard.ts now reads the config defensively, because it is loaded on the deny path too. A config read returning nothing previously would have crashed the security path, and a partial config must never be able to ENABLE a response action.

DIAGNOSTIC NOTE FOR FUTURE TESTS: while building this I found that evaluateToolCall returns allow with zero reasons when no threats directory is supplied, because rule loading degrades silently. Three of my own integration tests were initially vacuous for this reason. New guards assert that the rule bundle exists before relying on a verdict.

THE DESIGN INSIGHT: snapshot-on-deny cannot be rolled back into anything useful, because the blocked call never ran. The dangerous case is the mirror image — a destructive operation the runtime decided to ALLOW. So the response lifecycle needed a pre-operation snapshot on the allow path, which is what was missing.

WIRED: response-actions.ts gained runPreAllowedResponseActions (returns empty for any non-allow decision), PreOperationSnapshot, rollbackPreOperationSnapshot, commandTargetPath and isProtectedPath. rollback.ts gained createSnapshotDetailed (reporting every refused path with a reason: not_found / not_a_file / too_large / copy_failed, via lstat so a symlink is never followed into an unnamed location), bounded by maxBytesPerFile and maxTotalBytes, and rollbackSnapshot now falls back to metadata.json so a rollback works from a DIFFERENT process than the one that took it — which is the normal case. guard.ts gained GuardResult.snapshot, finalizeSnapshot, executeWithRollback, rollbackSnapshotFromGuardResult and GuardResult.signedChain.

SIGNED CHAIN: response-audit.ts gained logResponseActionToChain using its OWN existing Ed25519 + SHA-256 chain mechanism (no second implementation). signEntries is hard-coded true and ResponseAuditor.log already refuses to append unsigned, so a record is signed or absent; when the chain is unavailable the caller gets written:false plus a reason, NOTHING is appended, and the guard logs that the snapshot was not recorded. A rollback is recorded as action 'rollback', never as 'preserved a copy' — reporting it as a snapshot would tell the operator the opposite of the truth.

OFF BY DEFAULT, DOUBLY GATED: snapshot_before_destructive defaults false AND protect_paths defaults [] — even with the flag on, an empty list snapshots nothing, so guarding the whole filesystem was never possible. snapshot_retention_days defaults 7. response.audit.signed_chain defaults false, and its path is confined to ~/.singularity-aidr by the existing normalizeStateFilePath (a config outside it is reset with a warning), because untrusted config must not redirect security evidence.

THE BLOCK IS NEVER WEAKENED: every response-layer call sits inside the try/never-throws discipline, and a response failure is recorded as outcome:'failure' with the verdict untouched. A test proves that when the snapshot cannot be written the verdict stays allow and the failure is reported.

END-TO-END DEMONSTRATION with the REAL guard (no mocks), packages/core/scripts/demo-response-rollback.mts: STAGE 0 off by default — no actions, no snapshot, no files created. STAGE 1 enabled — snapshot success with snapshotId and bytes, target byte-identical after the guard, signed chain write {written:true, entryId}. STAGE 2 the allowed operation really deletes the target. STAGE 3 rollback restores it BYTE-IDENTICAL. STAGE 4 the chain holds two records where record2._prev_hash === record1._entry_hash, an independent fresh ResponseAuditor reports {valid:true}, and flipping one signed field flips it to {valid:false} naming the tampered entry. The plain log contains no file contents.

ROOT CAUSE ESTABLISHED (not a test-timeout issue at all): every connector's build script began with `pnpm -C ../core build`, whose first action is `rmrf dist`. Under `pnpm -r` those packages build CONCURRENTLY, so four processes deleted and recreated the same packages/core/dist tree at the same time. Anything importing core during that window failed with 'Failed to resolve entry for package @singularityrd/aidr-core'. The opencode contract tests looked like they were timing out at 30000ms; in fact the whole module graph failed to resolve under the churn. The suite was already green on a quiet tree, so the defect was build-ordering fragility rather than a product regression - but it made red runs untrustworthy.

FIX 1 (guard): new scripts/ensure-core-build.mjs builds core only when it is actually stale (required outputs missing, or a .ts input newer than the oldest required output). Every connector build script now calls the guard instead of unconditionally rebuilding core. Note: the freshness check must compare only .ts inputs, because core's own copy-generated step writes src/generated/*.json AFTER tsc runs, which otherwise makes sources look newer than outputs forever.

FIX 2 (sequencing): new scripts/build-workspace.mjs replaces `pnpm -r run build` as the root build. It compiles the AIG data, builds core exactly once to completion, then builds the remaining packages with AIDR_WORKSPACE_BUILD=1. In that mode the guard REFUSES to rebuild core rather than doing so under a sibling's bundler - which it previously did, surfacing as a misleading esbuild 'Cannot read file: packages/core/dist/index.js' in the extension package.

FIX 3 (latent defect the guard exposed): packages/cli consumed core but never depended on core being built, so a clean `pnpm build` failed with 5 TS2307 errors. It now runs the guard like the other consumers.

FIX 4 (deterministic gate): new scripts/run-tests-ci.mjs and `pnpm test:ci` build once and then run the suite with AIDR_TEST_NO_BUILD=1, which makes the Vitest global setup VERIFY artifacts instead of rebuilding them. vitest-global-setup.mjs was rewritten accordingly: it no longer runs a full per-process rebuild chain.
